headline: ReRAM technology addresses AI inference memory bottleneck; in-memory compute demos show 80x lower power than NVIDIA GPU; first mass production and first AI customer are key FY27 catalysts
reasoning: Hanoch explains that as AI shifts from training to inference, non-volatile memory becomes critical because inference requires fast, low-power memory that retains data without power. Existing flash memory cannot be manufactured at advanced geometries required by edge AI devices such as cars and robots. Weebit's ReRAM addresses the data-movement bottleneck where 60-80% of AI compute power and time is spent shuttling data between memory and processors. An in-memory compute demonstration with a US partner showed 80x lower power consumption than an NVIDIA GPU. Near-term milestones include first products reaching mass production and signing the first AI customer before end of calendar 2026, with commercial deals already closed with SMIC, Texas Instruments and DPI Tech.
quote: So you need to understand most compute engines today, they have a processing unit where the things are actually done and you have a memory which has all the data and data keeps moving back and forth from the processing, from the memory to the processing unit and back. Now today in AI, you have so much memory going back and forth that actually that the NVIDIA processors, as fast as they are, they just wait for data a lot of time. So it's becoming a real bottleneck that in the system the data isn't coming in fast enough, about 80%, sixty to 80% depending on the study that you read is being spent on just moving the data around both in terms of power consumption and in terms of time. So when you can put the computation in the memory... we had a company in the US that took our initial samples of this technology and tried them and analysed them and they saw a significant reduction in power consumption, 80 times lower power consumption than an NVIDIA GPU.
episode_title: AI’s memory bottleneck creating a new opportunity

headline: Semiconductors are the most important industry on the planet, yet Australia remains significantly underexposed with little local activity
reasoning: Coby Hanoch argued that semiconductors are the defining industry globally, noting that 9 of the top 10 market-cap companies in the world are semiconductor companies. He observed that Australia has been behind on this front with very little semiconductor activity domestically, making industry events like Semiconductor Australia 2026 important for raising awareness and building the local ecosystem.
quote: Semiconductors today is, I think I can say without a doubt it's the most important technology or industry on this planet. You know, 9 out of the top 10 market cap companies in the world are semiconductor companies. I think that Australia has been behind on this front. There really is not much semiconductor activity in Australia. So I think this conference is very important to bring semiconductor to the forefront and to expose it in Australia.
